title: by and until; by the time ...
subtitle: by Monday / until Monday
summary: Learn the difference between by (not later than) and until (how long something continues), and how to use by the time ... .

lesson.heading: by = not later than
lesson.text: **by** + a time means 'at or before that time, not later than that time'.

examples.text: I sent the documents today, so they should arrive **by Monday**.
We'd better hurry. We have to be home **by 5 o'clock**.
Where's Sarah? She should be here **by now**.
examples.note: = now or before now, so she should already be here

examples.text: This milk has to be used **by 14 August**.

lesson.heading: until = how long
lesson.text: We use **until** (or **till**) to say how long a situation continues.

examples.text: *A:* Shall we go now? *B:* No, let's wait **until it stops raining**.
I was very tired this morning. I stayed in bed **until half past ten**.
I didn't get up **until half past ten**.

lesson.heading: until or by?

left.label: until - a situation continues to that time

right.label: by - something happens not later than that time

lesson.note: Joe will be away until Monday = he'll be back on Monday. Joe will be back by Monday = not later than Monday.

lesson.heading: by the time something happens
lesson.text: You can say **by the time** + a clause. It means that something else will happen (or has happened) during the time in between.

examples.text: It's too late to go to the bank now. **By the time we get there**, it will be closed.
examples.note: it will close between now and the time we get there

examples.text: You'll need plenty of time at the airport. **By the time you check in** and go through security, it will be time for your flight.
Hurry up! **By the time we get to the cinema**, the film will already have started.

lesson.note: After by the time we use the present, not will.

lesson.heading: by the time something happened
lesson.text: You can use **by the time** for the past in the same way. The other action is often in the past perfect (**had left**, **had started**).

examples.text: Karen's car broke down on the way to the party. **By the time she arrived**, most of the other guests **had left**.
I had a lot of work to do yesterday evening. I was very tired **by the time I finished**.
It took us a long time to find somewhere to park. **By the time we got to the cinema**, the film **had already started**.

lesson.heading: by then / by that time
lesson.text: When the time is already clear, you can simply say **by then** or **by that time**.

examples.text: Karen finally got to the party at midnight, but **by then** most of the other guests had left.
examples.note: or ... but by that time, most of the other guests had left

lesson.text: Ask yourself: does the situation continue (*until*) or does something happen at some point before a deadline (*by*)?

exercises.prompt: I have to be at the airport not later than 8.30. In other words: I have to be at the airport ___.
exercises.explanation: by 8.30 = at or before 8.30, not later than 8.30.

exercises.prompt: Let me know ___ whether you can come to the party.
exercises.explanation: by + a day means 'on or before that day'.

exercises.prompt: Steve has gone away. He'll be away ___ Monday.
exercises.explanation: The situation (being away) continues to Monday, so we use until.

exercises.prompt: Sorry, but I must go. I have to be home ___ 5 o'clock.
exercises.explanation: This is a deadline: not later than 5 o'clock.

exercises.prompt: According to the forecast, the bad weather will continue ___ the weekend.
exercises.explanation: The bad weather continues all the way to the weekend, so we need until.

exercises.prompt: I'm still waiting for Tom to call me. He should have called me ___.
exercises.explanation: by now = now or before now, so it should already have happened.

exercises.prompt: Don't pay the bill today. Wait ___ tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Waiting continues up to tomorrow, so we use until.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Will you still be in the office at 6.30? *B:* No, I'll have gone home ___.
exercises.explanation: by then = at or before that time; the going home will already have happened.

exercises.statement: We have plenty of time. The film doesn't start by 8.30.
exercises.explanation: The film doesn't start until 8.30. The waiting continues to 8.30, so we need until.

exercises.prompt: I saw two men trying to steal a car and called the police, but it was some time before they came. By the time ___, the two men had disappeared.
exercises.explanation: by the time + past simple, with the past perfect (had disappeared) for what happened first.

exercises.prompt: You meant to catch a train, but it took you longer than expected to get to the station. Put the parts in order.
exercises.answer: By the time I got to the station, my train had already left.
exercises.explanation: The train left during the time it took you to get there.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with what you can say about it.
